source.title_on_document: Artificial Intelligence Enhances Human Creativity Through Real-Time Evaluative Feedback

supplement.where: PDF pp. 39-52, Supplementary Materials, supporting text, Tables S1-S9 and references; materials, data and analysis scripts are also linked at https://osf.io/6k52d/?view_only=398df4fd924440ee9387af4f6434d422 (PDF pp. 2, 15).
supplement.holds: Model training and validation and invalid-response screening (pp. 40-42); analyzed-sample demographics (Table S1, p. 43); self-rating/originality correlations (Tables S2 and S5, pp. 44, 47); full originality mixed-model coefficients and SEs (Tables S3 and S6, pp. 45, 48); mediation coefficients and confidence intervals (Tables S4 and S7, pp. 46, 49); squared-difference evaluation-accuracy models (Tables S8 and S9, pp. 50-51). These tables are included in this PDF. Cluster-robust check estimates are explicitly not reported (p. 18); analysis scripts are linked online rather than printed.

paper_design_summary: Study 1 compared Prolific adults generating design solutions under continuous GPT-3 numerical originality feedback, practice-only feedback, or no feedback; the paper specifies random task order but does not explicitly state random assignment to feedback conditions (PDF pp. 8-11). Study 2 randomly assigned museum visitors to immediate or delayed numerical feedback from AuDrA during drawing tasks (PDF pp. 12-14). Both studies scored the originality of human-produced outputs using the feedback model and also examined self-rating calibration; the feedback consisted only of numerical originality ratings (PDF pp. 20-28, 31).

studies.label: Study 1: online design-problem experiment; feedback assignment mechanism not stated

assignment.what_was_assigned: A between-participant feedback condition: continuous, practice-only intermediate, or no feedback. Only the sequence of design problems is explicitly described as random. This does not establish random assignment to AI assistance. Design is coded other pending confirmation, rather than assuming either randomized or nonrandom allocation (PDF p. 11).
assignment.quote: Condition was a between-participants factor with three levels (continuous feedback, intermediate feedback, no feedback).
assignment.locator: PDF p. 11, Procedure, lines 179-191; p. 12, Figure 2.
assignment.prereg_locator: PDF pp. 2 and 15, Open access statement and Transparency and openness: https://aspredicted.org/bgmj-yrm4.pdf. Reported deviations include adding the intermediate arm, changing the evaluation-accuracy analysis, and including non-engineers. The linked preregistration could not be retrieved in this job.

arms.name: Continuous feedback
arms.description: GPT-3 originality-score feedback during practice and all scored trials. Procedure reports 208 participants received this condition before the data-cleaning account; that number is not explicitly a randomized or analyzed count (PDF p. 11).

arms.name: Intermediate feedback (practice only)
arms.description: GPT-3 originality-score feedback during practice only, removed during scored trials. Procedure reports 214 participants received this condition before the data-cleaning account; that number is not explicitly a randomized or analyzed count (PDF p. 11).

arms.name: No feedback
arms.description: No originality feedback at any stage. Procedure reports 208 participants received this condition before the data-cleaning account; that number is not explicitly a randomized or analyzed count. All arms received repeated be-creative prompts (PDF p. 11).

participants.exclusions: The paper reports 629 recruited adults (PDF p. 8), not an explicit randomized total. Invalid ideas, fewer than 1% of 8,173 initial entries, were excluded; 11 participants were excluded for completion duration more than three SDs from the average; 56 for copy-and-paste indicators on over 25% of responses; 15 for using a mobile phone or tablet; and 34 trials for containing only one response (PDF pp. 15-16). Overlap among these exclusion categories is not specified. The final reported sample is 554 people providing 7,174 valid responses (p. 16). Participant counts conflict across sections, so arm-specific analyzed counts are left null; see open_questions.
participants.who: English-speaking adult Prolific volunteers with and without engineering experience (PDF p. 8). The final analyzed sample is aged 18-71 (PDF p. 16); Table S1 explicitly describes analyzed participants (PDF p. 43).
participants.country: United States; Canada; United Kingdom (PDF p. 8).
participants.locator: PDF p. 8, Method for Study 1, Participants; pp. 15-16, Data cleaning; p. 43, Table S1.

ai_tool.name_model: Fine-tuned GPT-3 davinci-002 (PDF p. 40, Supporting text).
ai_tool.how_used: A submitted human solution was sent to the scoring API; the returned originality score was normalized to 1-10 and displayed graphically, with the participant's own idea and rounded-down score. Feedback provided no generated ideas or qualitative suggestions (PDF pp. 9-10, 31). The fine-tuning used an existing design-idea corpus and expert ratings (PDF pp. 9, 40). The arm label generative_ai records the GPT-3 model family, while eligibility flags uncertainty about whether numerical-only prediction constitutes generative assistance under this codebook.

task.description: Generate solutions for clean-water access in remote areas, helping people with memory impairments remember important tasks, and pedestrian-crossing safety. Practice used remote-learning engagement and was not analyzed. Participants could submit up to 10 solutions per main problem and rated each solution themselves (PDF pp. 8-11).
task.duration: 6 minutes per main design problem (PDF p. 9); average total study duration 33.62 minutes (PDF p. 11).

outcomes.name: Originality of design solutions with continuous feedback
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Each submitted solution was scored by the fine-tuned GPT-3 model, with scores normalized to 1-10 (PDF pp. 9-10, Materials; p. 20, Reliability). The same model supplied the intervention feedback and the outcome score. Originality was analyzed at the response level using mixed models with participant and problem random intercepts, not participant averages (PDF pp. 16-18, Analysis strategy). The reported 7,174 responses are the full three-arm model dataset, not a count for this pairwise contrast alone (PDF p. 16). Table S3 contains the condition-only model and variants adding response/trial order and self-ratings; these are variants of the same outcome. Cluster-robust checks are described as convergent but their estimates are not printed (PDF p. 18). Originality is described as the primary hypothesis on PDF p. 21; a preregistered primary-outcome designation could not be independently checked. The model generated numerical scores only, making the intervention's fit to the generative-AI scope an adjudication issue (PDF p. 31).

contrasts.reported: Continuous feedback EMM = 6.67, SE = 0.15, 95% CI [6.34, 7.00]; control EMM = 6.13, SE = 0.15, 95% CI [5.79, 6.46]; t(8.50) = -3.56, p < .01; d = -0.35, SE = 0.10, 95% CI [-0.57, -0.13] (PDF p. 22). Table S3, Model 1: Condition (feedback) b = 0.54 (SE = 0.15), p < .001. The negative t and d are preserved as printed; the arm EMMs favor feedback. The discussion also reports the benefit as d = 0.35 (PDF p. 29).
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 22, Figure 3 caption and originality results; p. 45, Table S3, Model 1; p. 29, Discussion.

outcomes.name: Originality of design solutions after practice-only feedback was removed
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The intermediate arm received GPT-3 numerical originality feedback during practice and no feedback during the scored design-problem trials (PDF p. 11, Procedure; p. 12, Figure 2). The model still scored these outputs for analysis without displaying the feedback to this arm. This is the same originality measure and the same full three-arm model dataset of 7,174 responses as S1-O1, separated here because the intervention arm produced the analyzed outputs after feedback removal; it is not a new sample or an additional pool of outputs (PDF pp. 16-18). Counts for this arm or either pairwise contrast are not stated consistently. The continuous-feedback comparator in the second contrast retained feedback; ai_available_when_produced = no describes the intermediate treatment arm. Table S3 model variants and the exploratory mediation in Table S4 concern this same outcome. The intermediate condition was added after preregistration (PDF p. 15).

contrasts.reported: Intermediate feedback EMM = 6.80, SE = 0.15, interval [6.46, 7.13]; control EMM = 6.13, SE = 0.15, 95% CI [5.79, 6.46]; t(8.95) = -4.36, p < .01; d = -0.43, SE = 0.10, 95% CI [-0.66, -0.21] (PDF p. 22). Table S3, Model 1: Condition (intermediate) b = 0.67 (SE = 0.15), p < .001. The negative t and d are preserved as printed; the arm EMMs favor intermediate feedback. The discussion also reports this benefit as d = 0.43 (PDF p. 29).
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 22, Figure 3 caption and originality results; p. 45, Table S3, Model 1; p. 29, Discussion.

contrasts.reported: The continuous-versus-intermediate comparison is reported as d = 0.08, SE = 0.10, 95% CI [-0.14, 0.30]; t(3.80) = -0.86, p = .68. Intermediate EMM = 6.80, SE = 0.15; continuous EMM = 6.67, SE = 0.15. The paper's printed signs are retained without computing or reorienting an effect size.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 22, originality results, lines 435-440 and Figure 3 caption.

studies.label: Study 2: naturalistic museum drawing experiment with AuDrA numerical feedback

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individual museum visitors were assigned after a warm-up to immediate feedback after their first drawing or delayed feedback after two drawings. Assignment counts are stated in the procedure; first-drawing shape was also randomly selected (PDF p. 14). Condition was between people, with repeated drawings within people.
assignment.quote: participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: immediate or delayed feedback.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 14, Procedure, lines 249-263; p. 12, Figure 2.
assignment.prereg_locator: PDF p. 15, Transparency and openness, line 273: Study 2 was not preregistered. This explicit statement conflicts with the generic Preregistered analysis label on Table S9 (PDF p. 51).

arms.name: Immediate feedback
arms.description: AuDrA numerical originality feedback after the first drawing, before producing the second; continued feedback remained available. This is a non-generative scoring aid, coded other_aid (PDF pp. 12-14, 17, 29). Assigned and analyzed counts are on pp. 14 and 16.

arms.name: Delayed feedback (no feedback before the second drawing)
arms.description: No originality feedback until two drawings were completed; thereafter AuDrA feedback was supplied. It functions as the no-feedback comparator for the second-drawing contrast, despite receiving the scoring aid later (PDF pp. 14, 17; p. 47, Table S5 note). Assigned and analyzed counts are on pp. 14 and 16.

participants.exclusions: Drawings completed in 6 seconds or less, the bottom 3% of completion times, were excluded: 2,632 drawing entries. The final reported dataset contains 36,198 participants and 77,142 drawings, including 18,136 immediate-feedback and 18,062 delayed-feedback participants (PDF p. 16). The later restriction to the first two drawings per shape is described without a separate retained-person or retained-drawing count (PDF p. 17); a second-drawing-specific participant count is not reported.
participants.who: Visitors, including children, to a science museum Living Lab exhibit in Poland, recruited June 2023-June 2024 (PDF pp. 12-14). The total participating sample is 37,823 on p. 12, and the two explicitly assigned arm counts on p. 14 account for that total. The analyzed count is the cleaned sample explicitly reported on p. 16.
participants.country: Poland (study site; participant nationalities not stated), PDF p. 12.
participants.locator: PDF p. 12, Method for Study 2, Participants; p. 14, Procedure; pp. 16-17, Data cleaning and Analysis strategy.

ai_tool.name_model: AuDrA (Automated Drawing Assessment), a convolutional neural network for originality scoring (PDF pp. 6, 13, 29).
ai_tool.how_used: The API returned a numerical originality score for a submitted drawing. It appeared on a yellow vertical scale beside a green scale showing the participant's self-rating (PDF p. 13). The model evaluated human drawings rather than generating images or textual creative assistance. The opening sentence on p. 13 calls it a fine-tuned large language model, but the explicit AuDrA identification there and convolutional-network description on p. 29 identify the actual scoring model; this discrepancy is flagged for review.

task.description: Complete one of six unfinished shapes into something new and interesting on a touchscreen. A separate warm-up drawing preceded assignment. Participants could continue drawing and change shapes; the analysis focused on the first two drawings per shape (PDF pp. 12-14, 17).
task.duration: No time constraints on drawing completion (PDF p. 13).

outcomes.name: Originality of drawings, focusing on the second drawing after immediate versus delayed feedback
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: AuDrA scored the drawings and supplied numerical feedback; scores ranged from 0 to 10 (PDF pp. 13, 20). This is a convolutional scoring network, not a generative drawing tool (PDF p. 29). The primary comparison is the second drawing: the immediate arm had received feedback on its first drawing, while the delayed arm had not. Feedback was not withdrawn from the immediate arm, so this is not an after_ai assessment. The same outcome also has a baseline first-drawing comparison and an overall model pooling first and second drawings; those variants are retained below rather than counted as additional outcomes (PDF pp. 17, 22-24; Table S5 note on p. 47). ai_available_when_produced = mixed reflects the inclusion of unassisted first drawings in the reported overall analysis. Analyses use response-level mixed models with participant and shape random intercepts, and Table S6 adds response/trial order and self-rating variants (PDF pp. 16-18, 48). The paper reports 77,142 cleaned/analyzed drawings on p. 16 but subsequently restricts analysis to the first two drawings per shape on p. 17 without an explicit post-restriction or second-drawing observation count; n_units is therefore null for this outcome. Question with_ai describes feedback timing, not a judgment that this non-generative intervention meets scope.

contrasts.control_arm: Delayed feedback (no feedback before the second drawing)
contrasts.reported: Key second-drawing contrast: feedback EMM = 4.84, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [4.79, 4.90]; no feedback EMM = 4.44, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [4.40, 4.48]; t(54,419) = -11.83, p < .001; d = -0.20, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.24, -0.17] (PDF p. 24). Baseline first drawing: feedback EMM = 4.63, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [4.60, 4.67]; control EMM = 4.62, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [4.59, 4.66]; t(46,652) = -0.50, p = .62 (PDF p. 24). Overall first-and-second-drawing model: feedback EMM = 4.65, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [4.62, 4.68]; control EMM = 4.49, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [4.46, 4.52]; t(29,398) = -7.25, p < .001; d = -0.08, SE = 0.01, 95% CI [-0.10, -0.06] (PDF p. 23). Table S6, Model 1: Condition b = 0.16 (SE = 0.02), p < .001; Model 2: Response order x Condition b = 0.41 (SE = 0.03), p < .001. Negative t and d signs are as printed; higher EMMs favor immediate feedback. The discussion reports the second-drawing benefit as d = 0.20 (PDF p. 29).
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 22, Figure 3 caption; pp. 23-24, originality results; p. 48, Table S6, Models 1-2; p. 29, Discussion.

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: No reanalysis or shared intervention participants with another paper is stated. An existing design-idea corpus trained the Study 1 scoring model; the Study 2 human-rating validation used drawings from the present intervention sample. Neither establishes reuse of another paper's intervention participants.
sample_overlap.quote: The model was trained specifically for this study using an existing sample of design ideas
sample_overlap.locator: PDF p. 9, Development of AI feedback; p. 40, Supporting text; recruitment descriptions on pp. 8, 12-14.

company_involvement.description: No company affiliation or funding is reported. Affiliations are universities and a science centre, funding is from public research agencies, and the authors declare no conflicts of interest.
company_involvement.locator: PDF pp. 1-2, affiliations and Author Note.

eligibility.reason: Study 1 is the potential generative-AI study because its feedback system is fine-tuned GPT-3, but the PDF does not explicitly establish random assignment to its feedback arms: p. 11 states a between-participant factor and random task sequence only. Moreover, feedback consisted solely of numerical originality ratings, with qualitative generative feedback proposed as future work (PDF pp. 9-10, 31); inclusion of this use of an LLM requires scope adjudication. Study 2 explicitly randomized feedback timing (PDF p. 14), but its intervention was AuDrA, a convolutional scoring network, not a generative model (PDF pp. 6, 13, 29), so it cannot by itself establish a core generative-AI experiment. Both studies meet the size threshold in their reported cleaned samples: 554 and 36,198 people, respectively (PDF p. 16), and both computationally score originality of participant-produced outputs (PDF pp. 9, 13, 18, 20-24). No AI-versus-human-output comparison, observational adoption comparison, or synthesis is reported. Core is therefore unclear, not yes, pending the Study 1 assignment and numerical-feedback scope decisions.

one_line_finding: AI-scored originality was higher with continuous GPT-3 feedback (EMM 6.67 versus 6.13) and after practice-only feedback (6.80 versus 6.13; PDF p. 22), and for second drawings after immediate AuDrA feedback (4.84 versus 4.44; PDF p. 24).
open_questions: Was Study 1 feedback condition randomly assigned? The only randomization statement for Study 1 concerns problem order (PDF p. 11). The paper links a preregistration on pp. 2 and 15, but attempts to retrieve it and the named OSF repository through urllib with User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1 failed with WinError 10013 network restrictions. No external information was used.

Does numerical-only originality prediction from fine-tuned GPT-3 qualify as generative-AI assistance under this codebook? The intervention displayed scores only; the discussion proposes qualitative generative feedback as future work (PDF p. 31). AuDrA in Study 2 is explicitly a convolutional scoring model (PDF p. 29) and does not supply generated creative content.

Resolve Study 1 sample-count discrepancies before effect extraction: p. 8 reports 629 recruits, whereas p. 11 reports condition counts of 208, 214, and 208. The final sample is 554 on p. 16 and Figure 2; p. 16 lists 327 engineers and 228 non-engineers, whereas Table S1 on p. 43 lists 327 and 227. The condition-by-engineering counts on p. 16 also conflict with the stated total. Arm-specific analyzed counts and the randomized total have not been reconstructed.

What are the exact participant and drawing counts for Study 2 after restricting to the first two drawings per shape, and for the second-drawing contrast? PDF p. 16 gives the cleaned/analyzed corpus as 36,198 people and 77,142 drawings; p. 17 then describes the restriction without separate counts.

The PDF contains additional reporting inconsistencies: Study 2 is described as using a fine-tuned language model on p. 13 but is identified as AuDrA there and as a convolutional neural network on p. 29; Study 1 training-rater counts are 20 on pp. 9 and 40 versus 40 on p. 29; Study 2 validation-rater counts are 141 on pp. 13 and 40 versus 120 on p. 29. These rater samples are not counted as intervention participants.

Verify precision and effect-size conventions during extraction. The paper prints negative t and d values despite feedback arms having higher means (PDF pp. 22-24), gives positive benefit magnitudes in the discussion (p. 29), and does not clearly state the standardizer for d. The Study 2 SE/CI combinations and the differing SEs for the control intercept in Table S6 versus the post-hoc EMMs should be retained as printed until resolved.
notes: Screened on 2026-10-09. All page locators refer to physical PDF pages, including the cover and author note; the manuscript restarts printed page numbers for references/supplement. The entire markdown conversion, including references and supplement, was read in consecutive chunks; all recorded source statistics were checked against PDF text, and the four embedded figures were inspected in memory. No other screening form was opened. Outcome inventory from figures/tables: AI-scored originality of design solutions and drawings (Figures 1 and 3; Tables S3 and S6); participants' self-rated originality (PDF p. 20 and mediation Tables S4/S7); evaluation accuracy as self-rating/originality correlations and regression slopes (Figure 4, Tables S2/S5 and model variants in S3/S6), with squared-difference variants in Tables S8/S9. Self-ratings and calibration concern participants' judgments, not externally scored creativity/diversity of their produced work, so they are described here rather than counted as additional eligible output outcomes. Creative self-efficacy and perceived task difficulty were collected but not analyzed as focal outcomes in Study 1 (PDF p. 9); Table S1 familiarity/demographic comparisons and model validation/detection statistics are not creative-output intervention outcomes. No fluency, flexibility, usefulness, elaboration, convergent-test, or across-person diversity effect is reported. The discussions of homogenization cite other papers rather than analyze diversity in these samples (PDF p. 31). The two distinct originality measures yield three outcome entries because the practice-only Study 1 contrast answers after_ai. Model variants, mediation analyses, and baseline/overall Study 2 comparisons do not create additional outcome measures or participant samples. Validation raters and training corpora are documented as measurement development, not additional assistance experiments. No effects were calculated and no printed numbers were silently corrected. Main design class for the summary is other, referring to Study 1, the GPT-3 study with unconfirmed feedback randomization; Study 2 is a field_rct using non-generative AI.
